opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest concern is that it can make benchmark comparisons kind of meaningless if you're not careful. With test-time compute, you can often just keep throwing more inference at a problem: sample more, search longer, run majority voting over thousands of attempts. The score goes up, but that doesn't necessarily tell you the underlying model got smarter. It might just mean someone spent a hundred times more money per question.

So when you see a headline number, the first question should be: at what cost? A model that gets 80% using a dollar of compute per problem is very different from one that gets 85% using a thousand dollars per problem. I'd really like to see the field report results as a curve, performance as a function of compute, rather than a single point. That's the honest way to compare these systems.

There's also a subtler issue. Some techniques that scale with test-time compute rely on having a verifier, or on the benchmark having a single checkable answer. Math and coding with unit tests are like that. If you're doing best-of-N against something that effectively leaks the answer, you can inflate scores in ways that won't transfer to real-world tasks where you don't have a clean verifier. So you can end up optimizing for the structure of the benchmark rather than for the capability you actually care about.

To be clear, I'm very bullish on test-time compute. I think it's one of the most important directions in AI right now, and I've worked on it for years, going back to poker and Diplomacy, where search at inference time made a massive difference. But because it's so powerful, it's easy to misuse in evaluations. The capability is real; we just need to be more rigorous about how we measure it and report it.

r001.rationale: The response says higher scores may reflect spending more compute rather than a smarter model and recommends reporting performance-versus-compute curves. It does not clearly state that the apparent improvement can disappear when comparisons hold compute constant.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that concerns me most is that it makes benchmark numbers really hard to interpret. When you see a score, the question you should immediately ask is, how much compute was spent to get that number? Because if you're willing to throw a thousand times more compute at a problem, you can push a lot of benchmarks up substantially, and that's not necessarily a reflection of the model being smarter. It's a reflection of you having spent more money on that particular evaluation.

And I think there's a temptation, especially in a competitive environment, to report the best number you can get rather than the number that reflects how people would actually use the model. So you end up with these headline results that look impressive, but if you dig in, the cost per query might be something that no one would ever pay in practice. That's a bit misleading to the public and honestly to the research community too, because we're comparing apples to oranges.

The other thing I'd say is that benchmarks are a proxy. What we actually care about is whether the model can do useful things for people in the real world. And test-time compute is genuinely a real capability lever, I'm a big believer in it, but it has to be reported honestly. I think the right thing is to show the full curve, how performance scales with compute, rather than a single cherry-picked point. That gives you a much more complete picture of where a model actually stands.

r001.rationale: The response says extra compute can raise benchmark scores and make comparisons “apples to oranges,” but it does not state that apparent improvements can disappear when comparisons control for compute.

astra-6.text:
My main concern is that a benchmark score becomes hard to interpret if you don’t know how much compute went into producing it. You could get a higher score because the model is better, or because you gave it a hundred times more time to work on each problem. Those are both potentially useful, but they have very different implications for deployment.

So I’d like to see the performance curve: how well does the system do at different compute budgets, what does it cost, and how long does it take? There are problems where spending a lot of compute is absolutely worthwhile. But a single headline score doesn’t tell you whether that system is useful under the constraints people actually have.

r001.rationale: The response says higher scores may come from using much more compute, but it does not state that the apparent improvement disappears when comparisons control for compute.

sol-6.1.text:
One concern is that a benchmark score stops being very informative if you don’t know how much compute went into getting it. If one system gets one attempt and another generates a thousand answers and picks the best, those are very different comparisons. The second approach can still be useful, but you want to understand the cost and how the answer was selected.

I’m particularly wary of results where you generate lots of candidates and count the problem as solved if any candidate is correct. In practice, the user needs one answer, and identifying the correct one may be the hard part. I’d rather see performance as a function of compute, with the selection process included, than a single headline score.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark scores are hard to interpret without accounting for compute and recommends reporting performance by compute, but it does not state that apparent improvements can disappear when comparisons control for compute.
